rules.decision: When a probability survey supplies analysis weights, select and use the weight defined for the target population and measurement component rather than treating observations as equally weighted by default.
conditions: Sampling probabilities are unequal, oversampling occurred, or survey documentation provides weights
rules.action: Identify the survey-specific analysis weight and its construction/target from documentation. Preserve the weight alongside strata and PSU variables and use survey-aware estimation.
assumptions: The selected weight corresponds to the analysis population and variables
Survey documentation is available or the weighting scheme is otherwise known
warnings: Weights alone are not sufficient for complex-survey variance estimation.
Do not reconstruct a generic weight from the NHANES formula unless the target survey uses the same design.
NHANES-specific weight names and cycle-combination rules are not universal survey rules.
exceptions: A self-weighting simple random sample may not require unequal-probability weights, but its design still has to be declared.

source_evidence.support: Describes the multistage unequal-probability NHANES design and need to specify design parameters.
Explains base weights, nonresponse adjustment and post-stratification and relates base weight to selection probability.

rules.decision: Do not treat survey weights as sufficient for valid standard errors when the design also contains clustering or stratification.
conditions: PSUs/clusters, strata, differential weighting or other design features are present
rules.action: Use a survey-aware variance estimator with the available weight, strata and PSU/design variables. Carry design metadata into hypothesis tests and confidence intervals.
assumptions: Design variables correspond to the survey's documented sampling structure
warnings: Using weights in an ordinary iid estimator can still produce incorrect standard errors, tests and confidence intervals.
Do not infer that a large raw sample size makes clustering or stratification irrelevant.

source_evidence.support: States that weights affect parameter estimates while differential weighting, clustering and stratification affect variance estimates, standard errors, test statistics and confidence intervals.

rules.decision: For complex-survey subgroup/domain analysis, do not automatically delete all observations outside the target domain before variance estimation.
conditions: A complex survey is being analyzed
Taylor linearization or another design-based method requires the full design context
rules.action: Retain the eligible survey records needed by the variance estimator and specify the target domain with an indicator/subpopulation mechanism supported by the survey software.
assumptions: The survey software's domain-analysis method matches the design-based estimator being used
diagnostics: PSU and strata representation after domain definition
warnings: Naively subsetting to the target group can understate variance by treating the domain sample size as fixed.
Exact implementation is software- and design-specific.

source_evidence.support: NHANES guidance explains that Taylor-linearized domain variance requires all records with nonzero weights plus a domain indicator and warns that subsetting can underestimate variability.

rules.decision: Choose a missing-data strategy from the plausible missingness process, analysis target and available predictors, not from the percentage missing alone.
conditions: One or more variables required for analysis have missing values
rules.action: Describe where missingness occurs, identify variables associated with missingness and with incomplete values, assess whether MCAR/MAR assumptions are plausible, and state what unverifiable assumptions the primary analysis requires. Add sensitivity analysis when MNAR departures could materially change conclusions.
warnings: Do not encode 'missingness > X% = multiple imputation'.
MAR is an analysis assumption, not an empirically testable property that can be proven from observed data.
The same missing-data percentage can imply different risks under different mechanisms and estimands.

source_evidence.support: Explains MCAR/MAR/MNAR, the dependence of bias on why data are missing, inability to distinguish MAR from MNAR using observed data, and the role of sensitivity analysis.
source_evidence.section: Consequences of missing data / types of missing data

rules.decision: Do not automatically use mean imputation, missing-category indicators, last observation carried forward, or other single-imputation shortcuts as general missing-data solutions.
conditions: A simple single-value or indicator-based imputation strategy is proposed
rules.action: Block automatic recommendation unless a method-specific justification exists. Prefer a strategy whose assumptions and uncertainty treatment match the design and estimand.
diagnostics: Relationship between missingness and observed variables
warnings: Single imputation usually understates standard errors because uncertainty in the missing values is ignored.
A convenient imputation method can introduce bias even when the fraction missing is modest.
exceptions: Specialized deterministic rules may be justified by the data-generating process or protocol, but require explicit documentation.

source_evidence.support: States that common ad hoc methods including mean imputation, missing-category indicators and LOCF are not valid in general and that single imputation usually makes standard errors too small.
source_evidence.section: Statistical methods to handle missing data

rules.decision: When multiple imputation is used under a plausible MAR strategy, construct the imputation model to support the substantive analysis and the missingness assumptions.
conditions: Multiple imputation is selected as the missing-data strategy
rules.action: Include variables in the substantive analysis and, as feasible, observed variables predictive of the missing values and variables associated with the missingness process. Use variable-appropriate conditional imputation models, preserve compatibility with the substantive analysis, create multiple imputed datasets, pool analysis estimates and uncertainty across imputations, and inspect imputation-model behaviour rather than treating software completion as validation.
assumptions: The imputation model is compatible enough with the substantive analysis for the intended inference
The stated MAR-type assumptions are scientifically plausible
diagnostics: Distribution and plausibility of imputed values
Perfect-prediction or separation failures in categorical imputation models
warnings: Do not treat multiple imputation as automatically unbiased merely because software produced imputed datasets.
Do not use number or percentage missing as the sole reason to select multiple imputation.
MICE software convergence or completion does not by itself establish that the imputation model is scientifically or statistically adequate.
Perfect prediction in categorical imputation models can produce unstable or inappropriate imputations.
exceptions: MNAR analyses require additional assumptions and sensitivity models beyond an ordinary MAR imputation workflow.

source_evidence.support: Recommends including substantive-analysis variables and variables predictive of missing values or the missingness process to make MAR assumptions more plausible.
source_evidence.section: Plausibility of missing at random assumption

source_evidence.support: Royston and White describe the chained-equation algorithm, variable-specific imputation models, pooling with Rubin's rules, perfect-prediction problems, and the need to inspect imputation quality.

rules.decision: When data are clustered or multilevel, the imputation model must account for the multilevel structure rather than imputing as though all records were iid.
conditions: Data contain clusters, sites, centres, repeated hierarchical units or other multilevel structure
Missing values occur in variables used by the analysis
rules.action: Use or require a multilevel-compatible imputation strategy whose cluster structure is aligned with the substantive model. Distinguish variables missing within clusters from variables systematically absent in entire clusters.
assumptions: The imputation model is appropriate for variable types and hierarchy
diagnostics: Systematic versus sporadic missingness by cluster
warnings: Ignoring clustering during imputation can underestimate clustering and standard errors even if the final analysis later accounts for clustering.
A simple fixed-effect cluster indicator is not automatically equivalent to a valid multilevel imputation model.

source_evidence.support: Shows why clustered/multilevel missing data need specialized imputation and states that ignoring clustering can underestimate clustering and standard errors.
